opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the beginning I didn't try to convince people with arguments, because when something feels too fantastical, more talking just makes it sound even more like a fantasy. What worked was getting people to touch it themselves.

So the first thing I did was use it heavily myself, every day, for real work. I wasn't doing demos. I was debugging, reading code, writing small tools. Then when someone on the team was stuck on something, I'd just say, "Let's try it together," and sit next to them. Once they saw it actually solve a problem they cared about, not a toy problem, the attitude changed very quickly. That moment of "oh, it can really do this" is much more powerful than any slide.

The second thing was lowering the barrier. A lot of people's resistance isn't really skepticism, it's friction. They don't know how to set it up, what to ask, or how much to trust it. So we shared workflows internally: how you phrase a task, when you let it run on its own, when you step in and check. People learn much faster from a colleague's real example than from documentation.

And third, I tried to be honest about where it fails. If you oversell it, the first time it makes a mistake people feel cheated and go back to their old way. But if you tell them upfront, "It will get some things wrong, you still need to review," then when it does something impressive they're pleasantly surprised, and when it fails they're not disappointed. Trust builds gradually.

After a few weeks it kind of flipped. People who'd been skeptical started bringing me their own tricks. At that point you don't need to push anymore. The tool sells itself, and the culture just shifts. For me the lesson was that adoption of something new is less about the technology and more about giving people a safe, concrete first experience.

r001.rationale: The response describes personal use and trying the tool together, but does not mention a mandatory conversation quota.

r002.rationale: It discusses lowering setup and workflow friction, but does not say that already deployed instances were provided.

r003.rationale: It says colleagues learn from real examples and become more receptive, but does not clearly state that seeing others' successes sparks ideas for their own uses.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the hardest part wasn't the technology, it was the disbelief. When we first showed OpenClaude to the team, people's reaction was almost like watching a magic trick. They'd see it write a whole module, refactor it, run the tests, and they'd say, okay, that's a nice demo, but that's not how real work happens. There was this instinct to treat it as a toy, something you play with on a Friday afternoon and then go back to your actual job.

So I didn't try to convince anyone with arguments. I think if you argue with engineers about whether a tool is useful, you lose. What I did instead was very simple. I asked a few people, people who were already a bit curious, to use it for one real task they actually had on their plate that week. Not a demo task, not a benchmark, something with a deadline. And I said, if it wastes your time, tell me honestly and we'll stop.

What happened was that most of them came back and said, it didn't do everything, but it did the boring sixty percent, and I only had to fix the interesting forty. That's a very different story than "the AI writes code for you." That framing, that it takes away the tedious part, was something people could accept, because it didn't threaten their sense of what they were good at.

The second thing was that I used it myself, visibly. I think a lot of leaders talk about adopting AI tools but never actually touch them, and the team can smell that. I would share my sessions, including the ones where it went badly, where it confidently did the wrong thing and I had to pull it back. Showing the failures mattered more than showing the successes, because it made the whole thing feel real instead of fantastical. Fantastical is actually a problem. If something seems like magic, people don't trust it. Once it seemed like a slightly clumsy but very hardworking colleague, people started treating it like one.

And then it spread on its own. Someone would see a teammate close three tickets before lunch and ask what they were doing. I didn't have to mandate anything. I think the mistake would have been to make it a top-down rule in the first month. By the time we made it the default, most people were already there, and the ones who weren't just needed to see one task where it saved them an afternoon.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it would have been a mistake to mandate adoption; it does not describe a mandatory conversation quota.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes asking curious teammates to try OpenClaude on real tasks, but does not mention providing instances that were already deployed.

r003.rationale: The candidate says teammates saw someone close three tickets with OpenClaude and asked what they were doing, showing how others’ results prompted interest in using it.

astra-6.text: I think the key was to make it concrete. If you describe a big vision, people can feel that it’s too far away from their everyday work. So I’d start with one task they actually needed to do: try OpenClaude on that, see where it helps, and see where it fails. You don’t need everyone to believe the whole vision at once. You need them to have a useful experience, and then a reason to try it again. That’s how I’d approach building confidence—through small, practical results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key was to make it concrete. If you start by telling people how much it could change the way they work, it sounds too fantastical. So instead, you start with a task they already have: try using OpenClaude for this, and see whether it helps.

You don’t need everyone to believe in the whole vision immediately. You need them to have one useful experience, then another. And you have to leave room for skepticism—where does it work, where does it fail, what still requires your judgment? That’s how something gradually becomes part of people’s workflow.
